l: Force
In <color=#3366CC>physics</color>, a force is an action that can cause an <color=#3366CC>object</color> to change its <color=#3366CC>velocity</color> or its shape, or to resist other forces, or
to cause changes of pressure in a fluid. In <color=#3366CC>mechanics</color>, force makes ideas like pushing or pulling mathematically
precise. Because the <color=#3366CC>magnitude</color> and direction of a force are both important, force is a <color=#3366CC>vector</color> quantity (force vector).
The <color=#3366CC>SI unit</color> of force is the <color=#3366CC>newton (N)</color>, and force is often represented by the symbol F.
Force plays an important role in classical mechanics. The concept of force is central to all three of <color=#3366CC>Newton's laws of</color>

<color=#3366CC>motion</color>. Types of forces often encountered in <color=#3366CC>classical mechanics</color> include <color=#3366CC>elastic</color>, <color=#3366CC>frictional</color>, <color=#3366CC>contact or "normal" forces</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>gravitational</color>. The rotational version of force is <color=#3366CC>torque</color>, which produces <color=#3366CC>changes in the rotational speed</color> of an object.
In an extended body, each part applies forces on the adjacent parts; the distribution of such forces through the body is
the internal <color=#3366CC>mechanical stress</color>. In the case of multiple forces, if the net force on an extended body is zero the body is in
equilibrium.
In <color=#3366CC>modern physics</color>, which includes <color=#3366CC>relativity</color> and <color=#3366CC>quantum mechanics</color>, the laws governing motion are revised to rely on
<color=#3366CC>fundamental interactions</color> as the ultimate origin of force. However, the understanding of force provided by classical
mechanics is useful for practical purposes.
Development of the concept
Philosophers in <color=#3366CC>antiquity</color> used the concept of force in the study of <color=#3366CC>stationary</color> and moving objects and <color=#3366CC>simple machines</color>,
but thinkers such as <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color> and <color=#3366CC>Archimedes</color> retained fundamental errors in understanding force. In part, this was due
to an incomplete understanding of the sometimes non-obvious force of <color=#3366CC>friction</color> and a consequently inadequate view of
the nature of natural motion. A fundamental error was the belief that a force is required to maintain motion, even at a
constant velocity. Most of the previous misunderstandings about motion and force were eventually corrected by <color=#3366CC>Galileo</color>
<color=#3366CC>Galilei</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sir Isaac Newton</color>. With his mathematical insight, Newton formulated <color=#3366CC>laws of motion</color> that were not improved
for over two hundred years.
By the early 20th century, <color=#3366CC>Einstein</color> developed a <color=#3366CC>theory of relativity</color> that correctly predicted the action of forces on
objects with increasing momenta near the speed of light and also provided insight into the forces produced by
gravitation and <color=#3366CC>inertia</color>. With modern insights into <color=#3366CC>quantum mechanics</color> and technology that can accelerate particles
close to the speed of light, <color=#3366CC>particle physics</color> has devised a <color=#3366CC>Standard Model</color> to describe forces between particles smaller
than atoms. The <color=#3366CC>Standard Model</color> predicts that exchanged particles called <color=#3366CC>gauge bosons</color> are the fundamental means by
which forces are emitted and absorbed. Only four main interactions are known: in order of decreasing strength, they

are: <color=#3366CC>strong</color>, <color=#3366CC>electromagnetic</color>, <color=#3366CC>weak</color>, and <color=#3366CC>gravitational</color>. <color=#3366CC>High-energy particle physics</color> <color=#3366CC>observations</color> made during the 1970s
and 1980s confirmed that the weak and electromagnetic forces are expressions of a more fundamental <color=#3366CC>electroweak</color>
interaction.
Pre-Newtonian concepts
Since antiquity the concept of force has been recognized as integral to the functioning of each of the <color=#3366CC>simple machines</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>mechanical advantage</color> given by a simple machine allowed for less force to be used in exchange for that force
acting over a greater distance for the same amount of <color=#3366CC>work</color>. Analysis of the characteristics of forces ultimately
culminated in the work of <color=#3366CC>Archimedes</color> who was especially famous for formulating a treatment of <color=#3366CC>buoyant forces</color>
inherent in <color=#3366CC>fluids</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color> provided a <color=#3366CC>philosophical</color> discussion of the concept of a force as an integral part of <color=#3366CC>Aristotelian cosmology</color>. In
Aristotle's view, the terrestrial sphere contained four <color=#3366CC>elements</color> that come to rest at different "natural places" therein.
Aristotle believed that motionless objects on Earth, those composed mostly of the elements earth and water, were in
their natural place when on the ground, and that they stay that way if left alone. He distinguished between the innate
tendency of objects to find their "natural place" (e.g., for heavy bodies to fall), which led to "natural motion", and
unnatural or forced motion, which required continued application of a force. This theory, based on the everyday
experience of how objects move, such as the constant application of a force needed to keep a cart moving, had
conceptual trouble accounting for the behavior of <color=#3366CC>projectiles</color>, such as the flight of arrows. An archer causes the arrow to
move at the start of the flight, and it then sails through the air even though no discernible efficient cause acts upon it.
Aristotle was aware of this problem and proposed that the air displaced through the projectile's path carries the
projectile to its target. This explanation requires a continuous medium such as air to sustain the motion.
Though Aristotelian physics was criticized as early as the 6th century, its shortcomings would not be corrected until the
17th century work of <color=#3366CC>Galileo Galilei</color>, who was influenced by the late medieval idea that objects in forced motion carried
an innate force of impetus. Galileo constructed an experiment in which stones and cannonballs were both rolled down
an incline to disprove the Aristotelian theory of motion. He showed that the bodies were accelerated by gravity to an
extent that was independent of their mass and argued that objects retain their <color=#3366CC>velocity</color> unless acted on by a force, for
example <color=#3366CC>friction</color>. Galileo's idea that force is needed to change motion rather than to sustain it, further improved upon by
Isaac Beeckman, <color=#3366CC>René Descartes</color>, and Pierre Gassendi, became a key principle of Newtonian physics.
In the early 17th century, before Newton's <color=#3366CC>Principia</color>, the term "force" (Latin: vis) was applied to many physical and
non-physical phenomena, e.g., for an acceleration of a point. The product of a point mass and the square of its velocity
was named vis viva (live force) by <color=#3366CC>Leibniz</color>. The modern concept of force corresponds to Newton's vis motrix
(accelerating force).
Newtonian mechanics
Sir Isaac Newton described the motion of all objects using the concepts of <color=#3366CC>inertia</color> and force. In 1687, Newton published
his magnum opus, <color=#3366CC>Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica</color>. In this work Newton set out three laws of motion that
have dominated the way forces are described in physics to this day. The precise ways in which Newton's laws are
expressed have evolved in step with new mathematical approaches.
First law
Newton's first law of motion states that the natural behavior of an object at rest is to continue being at rest, and the
natural behavior of an object moving at constant speed in a straight line is to continue moving at that constant speed
along that straight line. The latter follows from the former because of the <color=#3366CC>principle that the laws of physics are the same</color>
for all <color=#3366CC>inertial observers</color>, i.e., all observers who do not feel themselves to be in motion. An observer moving in tandem
with an object will see it as being at rest. So, its natural behavior will be to remain at rest with respect to that observer,
which means that an observer who sees it moving at constant speed in a straight line will see it continuing to do so.
Second law
According to the first law, motion at constant speed in a straight line does not need a cause. It is change in motion that
requires a cause, and Newton's second law gives the quantitative relationship between force and change of motion.
<color=#3366CC>Newton's second law</color> states that the net force acting upon an object is equal to the <color=#3366CC>rate</color> at which its <color=#3366CC>momentum</color>
changes with <color=#3366CC>time</color>. If the mass of the object is constant, this law implies that the <color=#3366CC>acceleration</color> of an object is directly
proportional to the net force acting on the object, is in the direction of the net force, and is inversely proportional to the
<color=#3366CC>mass</color> of the object.

force by definition (balanced forces may be present nevertheless). In contrast, the second law states that if there is an

Third law
Whenever one body exerts a force on another, the latter simultaneously exerts an equal and opposite force on the first.
In vector form, if is the force of body 1 on body 2 and that of body 2 on body 1, then
This law is sometimes referred to as the action-reaction law, with called the action and the <color=#3366CC>reaction</color>.
Newton's third law is a result of applying <color=#3366CC>symmetry</color> to situations where forces can be attributed to the presence of
different objects. The third law means that all forces are interactions between different bodies. and thus that there is no
such thing as a unidirectional force or a force that acts on only one body.
In a system composed of object 1 and object 2, the net force on the system due to their mutual interactions is zero:
More generally, in a <color=#3366CC>closed system</color> of particles, all internal forces are balanced. The particles may accelerate with
respect to each other but the <color=#3366CC>center of mass</color> of the system will not accelerate. If an external force acts on the system, it
will make the center of mass accelerate in proportion to the magnitude of the external force divided by the mass of the
system.
Combining Newton's second and third laws, it is possible to show that the <color=#3366CC>linear momentum of a system is conserved</color> in
any <color=#3366CC>closed system</color>. In a system of two particles, if is the momentum of object 1 and the momentum of object 2, then
Using similar arguments, this can be generalized to a system with an arbitrary number of particles. In general, as long
as all forces are due to the interaction of objects with mass, it is possible to define a system such that net momentum is
never lost nor gained.
Defining "force"
Some textbooks use Newton's second law as a definition of force. However, for the equation for a constant mass to
then have any predictive content, it must be combined with further information. Moreover, inferring that a force is
present because a body is accelerating is only valid in an inertial frame of reference. The question of which aspects of
Newton's laws to take as definitions and which to regard as holding physical content has been answered in various
ways, which ultimately do not affect how the theory is used in practice. Notable physicists, philosophers and
mathematicians who have sought a more explicit definition of the concept of force include <color=#3366CC>Ernst Mach</color> and Walter Noll.
Combining forces
Forces act in a particular <color=#3366CC>direction</color> and have <color=#3366CC>sizes</color> dependent upon how strong the push or pull is. Because of these
characteristics, forces are classified as "<color=#3366CC>vector quantities</color>". This means that forces follow a different set of mathematical
rules than physical quantities that do not have direction (denoted <color=#3366CC>scalar</color> quantities). For example, when determining
what happens when two forces act on the same object, it is necessary to know both the magnitude and the direction of
both forces to calculate the <color=#3366CC>result</color>. If both of these pieces of information are not known for each force, the situation is
ambiguous.
Historically, forces were first quantitatively investigated in conditions of <color=#3366CC>static equilibrium</color> where several forces canceled
each other out. Such experiments demonstrate the crucial properties that forces are additive <color=#3366CC>vector quantities</color>: they
have <color=#3366CC>magnitude</color> and direction. When two forces act on a <color=#3366CC>point particle</color>, the resulting force, the resultant (also called the
<color=#3366CC>net force</color>), can be determined by following the parallelogram rule of <color=#3366CC>vector addition</color>: the addition of two vectors
represented by sides of a parallelogram, gives an equivalent resultant vector that is equal in magnitude and direction to
the transversal of the parallelogram. The magnitude of the resultant varies from the difference of the magnitudes of the
two forces to their sum, depending on the angle between their lines of action.
<color=#3366CC>Free-body diagrams</color> can be used as a convenient way to keep track of forces acting on a system. Ideally, these
diagrams are drawn with the angles and relative magnitudes of the force vectors preserved so that <color=#3366CC>graphical vector</color>
<color=#3366CC>addition</color> can be done to determine the net force.
As well as being added, forces can also be resolved into independent components at <color=#3366CC>right angles</color> to each other. A
horizontal force pointing northeast can therefore be split into two forces, one pointing north, and one pointing east.
Summing these component forces using vector addition yields the original force. Resolving force vectors into
components of a set of <color=#3366CC>basis vectors</color> is often a more mathematically clean way to describe forces than using
magnitudes and directions. This is because, for orthogonal components, the components of the vector sum are
uniquely determined by the scalar addition of the components of the individual vectors. Orthogonal components are
independent of each other because forces acting at ninety degrees to each other have no effect on the magnitude or
direction of the other. Choosing a set of orthogonal basis vectors is often done by considering what set of basis vectors
will make the mathematics most convenient. Choosing a basis vector that is in the same direction as one of the forces
is desirable, since that force would then have only one non-zero component. Orthogonal force vectors can be
three-dimensional with the third component being at right angles to the other two.
Equilibrium
When all the forces that act upon an object are balanced, then the object is said to be in a state of <color=#3366CC>equilibrium</color>. Hence,
equilibrium occurs when the resultant force acting on a point particle is zero (that is, the vector sum of all forces is
zero). When dealing with an extended body, it is also necessary that the net torque be zero. A body is in static
equilibrium with respect to a frame of reference if it at rest and not accelerating, whereas a body in dynamic equilibrium
is moving at a constant speed in a straight line, i.e., moving but not accelerating. What one observer sees as static
equilibrium, another can see as dynamic equilibrium and vice versa.
Static
Static equilibrium was understood well before the invention of classical mechanics. In an inertial reference frame,
objects that are not accelerating have zero net force acting on them.
The simplest case of static equilibrium occurs when two forces are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction. For
example, an object on a level surface is pulled (attracted) downward toward the center of the Earth by the force of
gravity. At the same time, a force is applied by the surface that resists the downward force with equal upward force
(called a <color=#3366CC>normal force</color>). The situation produces zero net force and hence no acceleration.
Pushing against an object that rests on a frictional surface can result in a situation where the object does not move
because the applied force is opposed by static friction, generated between the object and the table surface. For a
situation with no movement, the static friction force exactly balances the applied force resulting in no acceleration. The
static friction increases or decreases in response to the applied force up to an upper limit determined by the
characteristics of the contact between the surface and the object.
A static equilibrium between two forces is the most usual way of measuring forces, using simple devices such as
<color=#3366CC>weighing scales</color> and spring balances. For example, an object suspended on a vertical spring scale experiences the
force of gravity acting on the object balanced by a force applied by the "spring reaction force", which equals the object's
weight. Using such tools, some quantitative force laws were discovered: that the force of gravity is proportional to
volume for objects of constant <color=#3366CC>density</color> (widely exploited for millennia to define standard weights); <color=#3366CC>Archimedes' principle</color>
for buoyancy; Archimedes' analysis of the <color=#3366CC>lever</color>; <color=#3366CC>Boyle's law</color> for gas pressure; and <color=#3366CC>Hooke's law</color> for springs. These were
all formulated and experimentally verified before Isaac Newton expounded his <color=#3366CC>three laws of motion</color>.
Dynamic
Dynamic equilibrium was first described by <color=#3366CC>Galileo</color> who noticed that certain assumptions of Aristotelian physics were
contradicted by observations and <color=#3366CC>logic</color>. Galileo realized that <color=#3366CC>simple velocity addition</color> demands that the concept of an
"absolute rest frame" did not exist. Galileo concluded that motion in a constant <color=#3366CC>velocity</color> was completely equivalent to
rest. This was contrary to Aristotle's notion of a "natural state" of rest that objects with mass naturally approached.
Simple experiments showed that Galileo's understanding of the equivalence of constant velocity and rest were correct.
For example, if a mariner dropped a cannonball from the crow's nest of a ship moving at a constant velocity,
Aristotelian physics would have the cannonball fall straight down while the ship moved beneath it. Thus, in an
Aristotelian universe, the falling cannonball would land behind the foot of the mast of a moving ship. When this
experiment is actually conducted, the cannonball always falls at the foot of the mast, as if the cannonball knows to
travel with the ship despite being separated from it. Since there is no forward horizontal force being applied on the
cannonball as it falls, the only conclusion left is that the cannonball continues to move with the same velocity as the
boat as it falls. Thus, no force is required to keep the cannonball moving at the constant forward velocity.
Moreover, any object traveling at a constant velocity must be subject to zero net force (resultant force). This is the
definition of dynamic equilibrium: when all the forces on an object balance but it still moves at a constant velocity. A
simple case of dynamic equilibrium occurs in constant velocity motion across a surface with <color=#3366CC>kinetic friction</color>. In such a
situation, a force is applied in the direction of motion while the kinetic friction force exactly opposes the applied force.
This results in zero net force, but since the object started with a non-zero velocity, it continues to move with a non-zero
velocity. Aristotle misinterpreted this motion as being caused by the applied force. When kinetic friction is taken into
consideration it is clear that there is no net force causing constant velocity motion.
Examples of forces in classical mechanics
Some forces are consequences of the fundamental ones. In such situations, idealized models can be used to gain
physical insight. For example, each solid object is considered a <color=#3366CC>rigid body</color>.
Gravitational force or Gravity
What we now call gravity was not identified as a universal force until the work of Isaac Newton. Before Newton, the
tendency for objects to fall towards the Earth was not understood to be related to the motions of celestial objects.
Galileo was instrumental in describing the characteristics of falling objects by determining that the <color=#3366CC>acceleration</color> of every
object in <color=#3366CC>free-fall</color> was constant and independent of the mass of the object. Today, this <color=#3366CC>acceleration due to gravity</color>
towards the surface of the Earth is usually designated as and has a magnitude of about 9.81 <color=#3366CC>meters</color> per second
squared (this measurement is taken from sea level and may vary depending on location), and points toward the center
of the Earth. This observation means that the force of gravity on an object at the Earth's surface is directly proportional
to the object's mass. Thus an object that has a mass of will experience a force:
For an object in free-fall, this force is unopposed and the net force on the object is its weight. For objects not in free-fall,
the force of gravity is opposed by the reaction forces applied by their supports. For example, a person standing on the
ground experiences zero net force, since a <color=#3366CC>normal force</color> (a reaction force) is exerted by the ground upward on the
person that counterbalances his weight that is directed downward.
Newton's contribution to gravitational theory was to unify the motions of heavenly bodies, which Aristotle had assumed
were in a natural state of constant motion, with falling motion observed on the Earth. He proposed a <color=#3366CC>law of gravity</color> that
could account for the celestial motions that had been described earlier using <color=#3366CC>Kepler's laws of planetary motion</color>.
Newton came to realize that the effects of gravity might be observed in different ways at larger distances. In particular,
Newton determined that the acceleration of the Moon around the Earth could be ascribed to the same force of gravity if
the acceleration due to gravity decreased as an <color=#3366CC>inverse square law</color>. Further, Newton realized that the acceleration of a
body due to gravity is proportional to the mass of the other attracting body. Combining these ideas gives a formula that

This formula was powerful enough to stand as the basis for all subsequent descriptions of motion within the <color=#3366CC>Solar</color>
<color=#3366CC>System</color> until the 20th century. During that time, sophisticated methods of <color=#3366CC>perturbation analysis</color> were invented to

calculate the deviations of <color=#3366CC>orbits</color> due to the influence of multiple bodies on a <color=#3366CC>planet</color>, <color=#3366CC>moon</color>, <color=#3366CC>comet</color>, or <color=#3366CC>asteroid</color>. The

observed.
Electromagnetic
The <color=#3366CC>electrostatic force</color> was first described in 1784 by Coulomb as a force that existed intrinsically between two <color=#3366CC>charges</color>.
The properties of the electrostatic force were that it varied as an <color=#3366CC>inverse square law</color> directed in the <color=#3366CC>radial direction</color>, was
both attractive and repulsive (there was intrinsic polarity), was independent of the mass of the charged objects, and
followed the <color=#3366CC>superposition principle</color>. <color=#3366CC>Coulomb's law</color> unifies all these observations into one succinct statement.
Subsequent mathematicians and physicists found the construct of the <color=#3366CC>electric field</color> to be useful for determining the
electrostatic force on an electric charge at any point in space. The electric field was based on using a hypothetical "<color=#3366CC>test</color>
<color=#3366CC>charge</color>" anywhere in space and then using Coulomb's law to determine the electrostatic force. Thus the electric field
anywhere in space is defined as
where is the magnitude of the hypothetical test charge. Similarly, the idea of the <color=#3366CC>magnetic field</color> was introduced to
express how magnets can influence one another at a distance. The <color=#3366CC>Lorentz force law</color> gives the force upon a body with
charge due to electric and magnetic fields:
where is the electromagnetic force, is the electric field at the body's location, is the magnetic field, and is the <color=#3366CC>velocity</color> of
the particle. The magnetic contribution to the Lorentz force is the <color=#3366CC>cross product</color> of the velocity vector with the magnetic
field.
The origin of electric and magnetic fields would not be fully explained until 1864 when <color=#3366CC>James Clerk Maxwell</color> unified a
number of earlier theories into a set of 20 scalar equations, which were later reformulated into 4 vector equations by
<color=#3366CC>Oliver Heaviside</color> and <color=#3366CC>Josiah Willard Gibbs</color>. These "<color=#3366CC>Maxwell's equations</color>" fully described the sources of the fields as
being stationary and moving charges, and the interactions of the fields themselves. This led Maxwell to discover that
electric and magnetic fields could be "self-generating" through a <color=#3366CC>wave</color> that traveled at a speed that he calculated to be
the <color=#3366CC>speed of light</color>. This insight united the nascent fields of electromagnetic theory with <color=#3366CC>optics</color> and led directly to a
complete description of the <color=#3366CC>electromagnetic spectrum</color>.
Normal
When objects are in contact, the force directly between them is called the normal force, the component of the total force
in the system exerted normal to the interface between the objects. The normal force is closely related to Newton's third
law. The normal force, for example, is responsible for the structural integrity of tables and floors as well as being the
force that responds whenever an external force pushes on a solid object. An example of the normal force in action is
the impact force on an object crashing into an immobile surface.
Friction
Friction is a force that opposes relative motion of two bodies. At the macroscopic scale, the frictional force is directly
related to the normal force at the point of contact. There are two broad classifications of frictional forces: static friction
and <color=#3366CC>kinetic friction</color>.
The static friction force will exactly oppose forces applied to an object parallel to a surface up to the limit specified by
the <color=#3366CC>coefficient of static friction</color> multiplied by the normal force. In other words, the magnitude of the static friction force
satisfies the inequality:

Tension
Tension forces can be modeled using ideal strings that are massless, frictionless, unbreakable, and do not stretch.
They can be combined with ideal <color=#3366CC>pulleys</color>, which allow ideal strings to switch physical direction. Ideal strings transmit
tension forces instantaneously in action–reaction pairs so that if two objects are connected by an ideal string, any force
directed along the string by the first object is accompanied by a force directed along the string in the opposite direction
by the second object. By connecting the same string multiple times to the same object through the use of a
configuration that uses movable pulleys, the tension force on a load can be multiplied. For every string that acts on a
load, another factor of the tension force in the string acts on the load. Such machines allow a <color=#3366CC>mechanical advantage</color> for
a corresponding increase in the length of displaced string needed to move the load. These tandem effects result
ultimately in the <color=#3366CC>conservation of mechanical energy</color> since the work done on the load is the same no matter how
complicated the machine.
Spring
A simple elastic force acts to return a <color=#3366CC>spring</color> to its natural length. An <color=#3366CC>ideal spring</color> is taken to be massless, frictionless,
unbreakable, and infinitely stretchable. Such springs exert forces that push when contracted, or pull when extended, in
proportion to the displacement of the spring from its equilibrium position. This linear relationship was described by
<color=#3366CC>Robert Hooke</color> in 1676, for whom <color=#3366CC>Hooke's law</color> is named. If is the displacement, the force exerted by an ideal spring

Continuum mechanics
Newton's laws and Newtonian mechanics in general were first developed to describe how forces affect idealized <color=#3366CC>point</color>
<color=#3366CC>particles</color> rather than three-dimensional objects. In real life, matter has extended structure and forces that act on one
part of an object might affect other parts of an object. For situations where lattice holding together the atoms in an
object is able to flow, contract, expand, or otherwise change shape, the theories of <color=#3366CC>continuum mechanics</color> describe the

Fictitious
There are forces that are <color=#3366CC>frame dependent</color>, meaning that they appear due to the adoption of non-Newtonian (that is,

<color=#3366CC>non-inertial</color>) <color=#3366CC>reference frames</color>. Such forces include the <color=#3366CC>centrifugal force</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Coriolis force</color>. These forces are
considered fictitious because they do not exist in frames of reference that are not accelerating. Because these forces
are not genuine they are also referred to as "pseudo forces".
In <color=#3366CC>general relativity</color>, <color=#3366CC>gravity</color> becomes a fictitious force that arises in situations where spacetime deviates from a flat
geometry.

Potential energy
Instead of a force, often the mathematically related concept of a <color=#3366CC>potential energy</color> field is used. For instance, the
gravitational force acting upon an object can be seen as the action of the <color=#3366CC>gravitational field</color> that is present at the
object's location. Restating mathematically the definition of energy (via the definition of <color=#3366CC>work</color>), a potential scalar field is
defined as that field whose <color=#3366CC>gradient</color> is equal and opposite to the force produced at every point:
Forces can be classified as <color=#3366CC>conservative</color> or nonconservative. Conservative forces are equivalent to the gradient of a
potential while nonconservative forces are not.
Conservation
A conservative force that acts on a <color=#3366CC>closed system</color> has an associated mechanical work that allows energy to convert
only between <color=#3366CC>kinetic</color> or <color=#3366CC>potential</color> forms. This means that for a closed system, the net mechanical energy is conserved
whenever a conservative force acts on the system. The force, therefore, is related directly to the difference in potential
energy between two different locations in space, and can be considered to be an artifact of the potential field in the
same way that the direction and amount of a flow of water can be considered to be an artifact of the <color=#3366CC>contour map</color> of the
elevation of an area.
Conservative forces include <color=#3366CC>gravity</color>, the <color=#3366CC>electromagnetic</color> force, and the <color=#3366CC>spring</color> force. Each of these forces has models
that are dependent on a position often given as a <color=#3366CC>radial vector</color> emanating from spherically symmetric potentials.

For certain physical scenarios, it is impossible to model forces as being due to a simple gradient of potentials. This is
often due a macroscopic statistical average of <color=#3366CC>microstates</color>. For example, static friction is caused by the gradients of
numerous electrostatic potentials between the <color=#3366CC>atoms</color>, but manifests as a force model that is independent of any
macroscale position vector. Nonconservative forces other than friction include other contact forces, <color=#3366CC>tension</color>,
<color=#3366CC>compression</color>, and <color=#3366CC>drag</color>. For any sufficiently detailed description, all these forces are the results of conservative ones
since each of these macroscopic forces are the net results of the gradients of microscopic potentials.
The connection between macroscopic nonconservative forces and microscopic conservative forces is described by
detailed treatment with <color=#3366CC>statistical mechanics</color>. In macroscopic closed systems, nonconservative forces act to change the
<color=#3366CC>internal energies</color> of the system, and are often associated with the transfer of heat. According to the <color=#3366CC>Second law of</color>
<color=#3366CC>thermodynamics</color>, nonconservative forces necessarily result in energy transformations within closed systems from
ordered to more random conditions as <color=#3366CC>entropy</color> increases.
Units
The <color=#3366CC>SI</color> unit of force is the <color=#3366CC>newton</color> (symbol N), which is the force required to accelerate a one kilogram mass at a rate of
one meter per second squared, or kg·m·s2.The corresponding <color=#3366CC>CGS</color> unit is the dyne, the force required to accelerate a
one gram mass by one centimeter per second squared, or g·cm·s2. A newton is thus equal to 100,000 dynes.
The gravitational <color=#3366CC>foot-pound-second</color> <color=#3366CC>English unit</color> of force is the <color=#3366CC>pound-force</color> (lbf), defined as the force exerted by
gravity on a <color=#3366CC>pound-mass</color> in the <color=#3366CC>standard gravitational</color> field of 9.80665 m·s2. The pound-force provides an alternative
unit of mass: one <color=#3366CC>slug</color> is the mass that will accelerate by one foot per second squared when acted on by one
pound-force. An alternative unit of force in a different foot–pound–second system, the absolute fps system, is the
poundal, defined as the force required to accelerate a one-pound mass at a rate of one foot per second squared.
The pound-force has a metric counterpart, less commonly used than the newton: the <color=#3366CC>kilogram-force</color> (kgf) (sometimes
kilopond), is the force exerted by standard gravity on one kilogram of mass. The kilogram-force leads to an alternate,
but rarely used unit of mass: the metric slug (sometimes mug or hyl) is that mass that accelerates at 1 m·s2 when
subjected to a force of 1 kgf. The kilogram-force is not a part of the modern SI system, and is generally deprecated,
sometimes used for expressing aircraft weight, jet thrust, bicycle spoke tension, torque wrench settings and engine
output torque.
See also Ton-force.
Revisions of the force concept
At the beginning of the 20th century, new physical ideas emerged to explain experimental results in astronomical and
submicroscopic realms. As discussed below, relativity alters the definition of momentum and quantum mechanics
reuses the concept of "force" in microscopic contexts where Newton's laws do not apply directly.
Special theory of relativity

accelerate an object). When an object's velocity increases, so does its energy and hence its mass equivalent (inertia). It
thus requires more force to accelerate it the same amount than it did at a lower velocity. Newton's second law,
remains valid because it is a mathematical definition. But for momentum to be conserved at relativistic relative velocity,
